strengths: Addresses a well-motivated, practical problem overlooked by prior work: communication overhead dominates latency (58.55-93.47%) in bandwidth-constrained environments, making existing methods impractical for edge deployment
Clear presentation with comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions (bandwidth 10-500 Mbps, devices 2-8, sequence length 256-4096) on both vision (ViT) and NLP (GPT2) tasks
Solid technical design combining mixed-precision attention, NAVQ, and distributed class tokens; each component is well-motivated and includes theoretical justification
Impressive practical results: achieves 2.64× speedup over single-device and 15.25× over state-of-the-art methods at 10 Mbps where all baselines fail; 171.82× speedup over sequence parallelism
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 5-6) demonstrating contribution of each component; noise magnitude λ improves accuracy by 0.86%, distributed class tokens by 0.37-7.13%
Honest reporting of limitations including concerning zero-shot generalization degradation on GPT2 (43.22 → 62.29 perplexity); transparency strengthens credibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (sequence parallelism, vector quantization from VQVAE); NAVQ is straightforward noise injection without deep innovation; main novelty is application rather than method

Significant accuracy degradation concerns: 3.58% drop on ViT-Base with maximum compression (92.53% → 88.95%); critically, zero-shot generalization fails substantially, limiting applicability to domain-shifted scenarios
Experimental scope limited to small models (ViT-Base, GPT2-Small/Medium); scalability to modern large models (7B+, ViT-Large) remains unclear; vector quantization may not scale effectively

Simulated rather than real-world deployment: bandwidth capping on powerful GPUs (1660Ti) doesn't capture actual edge device constraints, network variability, latency variance, or wireless dynamics; no evaluation on true edge devices (mobile, IoT, Raspberry Pi)

Theoretical justifications make strong, unvalidated assumptions: Theorem 1 assumes i.i.d. Gaussian quantization errors across dimensions; Theorem 2's first-order Taylor expansion of softmax may be inaccurate for large quantization errors; results provide intuition but not practical guarantees

Unfair baseline comparisons: existing methods don't incur accuracy loss while ASTRA does; speedup numbers conflate computation gains with accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs; missing comparisons against quantized baselines or hybrid compression strategies

Codebook overhead underexplored: grouped VQ (G=32) requires separate codebooks per group; with 32 groups × 12 layers, storage overhead (~1GB) is significant for edge devices; synchronization protocol unspecified

Design choices lack principled justification: why G=32 optimal unclear; commitment loss weight β is finicky (0.1-1.67% accuracy drops with misconfiguration); λ=1.0 chosen empirically without guidance for different compression regimes
Missing critical ablations: no comparison of mixed-precision vs. uniform quantization; unclear if mixed-precision design is necessary or if simpler approaches suffice
Unaddressed practical concerns: device heterogeneity (asymmetric bandwidths), fault tolerance, codebook synchronization across devices, cost of averaging distributed class tokens not analyzed

strengths: Clear problem motivation with quantified evidence that communication dominates latency (58.55-93.47%) in bandwidth-constrained settings, addressing a genuine practical concern

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (ViT, GPT2), datasets (CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, Wikipedia, Wikitext-103), and dimensions (bandwidth, device count, sequence length) with thorough ablations
Honest acknowledgment of limitations, particularly the significant zero-shot generalization degradation (44% PPL increase for GPT2-M), showing integrity in presenting results
Practical relevance for edge deployment scenarios where bandwidth is genuinely constrained
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The approach combines existing techniques (vector quantization, noise-based regularization from Vicinal Risk Minimization, distributed class tokens) with the main contribution (mixed-precision attention) being relatively straightforward engineering

Weak theoretical contributions: Theorem 1 assumes quantization errors are i.i.d. Gaussian (unjustified for deterministic VQ), only provides relative guarantees, and ignores distribution shift at inference when noise is removed. Theorem 2 uses first-order Taylor expansion invalid under 2457× compression and assumes Gaussian independent errors contradicting structured quantization errors

Substantial accuracy degradation in critical settings: Zero-shot GPT2-M shows 43.22→62.29 PPL (~44% increase), CIFAR-100 shows 3.58% drop at G=1. Authors attribute this to 'limited expressiveness' but provide no solution, severely limiting practical applicability

Overstated claims: 'Up to 15.25× speedups' refers only to comparison with Sequence Parallelism which itself achieves 0.2× (slower than baseline). Meaningful speedups of 2.64× only at unrealistic 10 Mbps; at 100 Mbps, speedup drops to ~1.5×. Modern WiFi 6/6E provides 300+ Mbps, reducing the method's relevance

Reproducibility issues: Code availability not provided despite open-source claim; bandwidth simulation method unspecified; codebook synchronization across devices not discussed; extensive hyperparameter tuning (β, λ) without full grid search details; potential test set overfitting with multiple tuned hyperparameters

Limited baseline comparisons: Missing comparisons with simple baselines (uniform quantization of all embeddings vs. mixed-precision, low-rank approximation, sparse attention), and existing baselines may be suboptimal for low-bandwidth. No comparison with other compression techniques (pruning + sequence parallelism)

Narrow scope: Only classification and next-token prediction; no generation tasks; tested only on ViT and GPT2-Small/Medium; assumes scenarios becoming less common as network speeds improve; distributed robustness and synchronization overhead not analyzed

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies and quantifies a genuine bottleneck (communication accounting for 58.55-93.47% of latency in bandwidth-constrained settings) that existing multi-device inference methods fail to address

Novel technical contributions: Mixed-Precision Attention mechanism is elegant and well-motivated; Noise-Augmented Vector Quantization creatively applies VRM principle; Distributed Class Tokens addresses real information asymmetry issues
Strong theoretical justification: Theorems 1-2 provide formal backing via Wasserstein distance and variance reduction guarantees, lending rigor to design choices

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple architectures (ViT-Base, GPT2-S/M), domains (vision and NLP), systematic variation of bandwidth (10-500 Mbps), device counts (2-8), and sequence lengths (256-4096) with thorough ablations

Compelling empirical results: Achieves 2.64× speedup over single-device and 15.25× over state-of-the-art under extreme bandwidth constraints (10 Mbps) while maintaining <3.58% accuracy degradation under 2457.6× compression
Honest and transparent reporting: Explicitly acknowledges zero-shot generalization limitations, provides detailed ablation studies, includes impact statement and limitations discussion
Clear presentation: Well-organized writing, effective visualizations (especially Figure 3's latency breakdown), and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Significant zero-shot generalization degradation for language models: GPT2-M zero-shot perplexity increases 44.1% (43.22→62.29), substantially limiting applicability. While acknowledged, no concrete solutions proposed beyond future work speculation

Gap between simulation and real deployment: Bandwidth constraints simulated via software caps; real wireless effects (latency variability, jitter, packet loss, interference) not modeled. Codebook synchronization and adaptation in truly heterogeneous distributed settings not addressed

Limited model scale: All experiments on relatively small models (ViT-Base ~86M, GPT2-Small/Medium ~124-355M). Scalability to billion-parameter models currently in production is unclear; unclear if approach generalizes beyond small models

Restrictive theoretical assumptions: Theorem 1 assumes i.i.d. Gaussian quantization errors (contradicting deterministic nature of quantization); Theorem 2 uses first-order Taylor approximation that may break down under extreme compression; practical applicability of bounds questionable

Incomplete codebook management analysis: Multiple codebooks required for grouped VQ (G=32) increase storage overhead, but concrete numbers not provided. Codebook sharing, synchronization, and initialization costs in heterogeneous settings not discussed

Ad-hoc hyperparameter selection: Multiple hyperparameters (λ, β, G, K) with limited principled guidance for new models/datasets; fine-tuning epochs vary significantly across tasks without clear justification; selection procedures not well-documented

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Baseline methods not equipped with similar compression techniques for fair comparison. Applying post-hoc quantization to baselines would strengthen claims regarding superiority of the proposed approach
Reproducibility and documentation gaps: Code link redacted; fine-tuning procedures vary across tasks; limited pseudocode for NAVQ training; some implementation details unclear for exact reproduction

Missing practical considerations: Synchronization overhead in distributed settings not analyzed; no discussion of fault tolerance or communication failures; real-time bandwidth adaptation not addressed; assumes homogeneous device capabilities

Unclear theoretical-practical gap: Quantization error in practice is deterministic and structured, not i.i.d. random as assumed in proofs; impact of first-order approximation violations under aggressive compression not empirically validated
